context: Launch day is a week away. Your speechwriter shuts the door and asks the one question the speech has to answer: why do you actually want to be president?
prompt: No cameras, no notes, nobody to impress. What is the true answer?

options.label: Because I would be better at it than anyone alive.
options.receipt: Asked in private why you wanted it, you said you would be better at it than anyone alive.

options.label: Because it is broken, and nobody else is going to fix it.
options.receipt: Asked why you wanted it, you said it was broken and no one else was going to fix it.

options.label: Because I have wanted it since I was nine years old.
options.receipt: Asked why you wanted to be president, you said you had wanted it since you were nine.

options.label: Because certain people said I never could.
options.receipt: Asked why you were running, you gave the true reason: certain people said you never could.

context: The senator who gave you your first job, taught you everything you know and still calls you kid wants to run too. There is room in this lane for exactly one of you.
prompt: What do you do about your mentor? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: Announce first. She taught me to move fast.
options.receipt: Your mentor still called you kid. You announced first and let her read about it.

options.label: Go to her house. Ask for her blessing, and mean it.
options.receipt: Your mentor wanted the same race. You drove to her house and asked for her blessing.

options.label: Stand down. I owe her, and I can wait four years.
options.receipt: Your mentor wanted the same race. You stood down and called it gratitude. Four years is a long time to be grateful.

options.label: Praise her in public. Sign her donors in private.
options.receipt: You praised your mentor from the podium while your finance chair worked through her donor list.

context: Your team offers two launches. One is safe, forgettable and cannot hurt you. The other is a stunt that makes you a star by dinner or a punchline by breakfast.
prompt: How much of the campaign do you bet on day one?

slider.right: All of it. Star or punchline
slider.centre: Half. A stunt with a safety net

context: Before you file the paperwork to run, your oldest adviser wants straight answers. Nobody else will ever see them.
prompt: An honesty check. Is each one true of you? Yes or no, four seconds each.

cards.text: I have practiced my signature for the bill signings.
I remember exactly who laughed when I first said I would run.
I would rather lose big than never find out.
I assume someone on my own team is already leaking.
I could lose this race and still be a happy person.
I have forgiven someone who never apologized.
People usually leave a conversation with me agreeing.
I would crawl to win over a powerful person who despises me.

context: A 23-year-old field organizer sent your volunteers to the wrong caucus site. You lost the county by eleven votes. She is crying in the hallway, and the whole staff is watching to see what you do.
prompt: What do you do with her?

options.label: Fire her in the hallway. The staff need to see a price.
options.receipt: A 23-year-old cost you a county by eleven votes. You fired her in the hallway so the others could watch.

options.label: Keep her. Nobody alive will check an address harder.
options.receipt: A 23-year-old cost you a county by eleven votes. You kept her. Nobody on your staff has forgotten it.

options.label: Keep her, somewhere she can never hurt me again.
options.receipt: She cost you a county, so you kept her on the payroll and off the map.

options.label: Tell the press the mistake was mine. She is 23.
options.receipt: A 23-year-old lost you a county, and you told the press the mistake was yours.

context: A New Hampshire diner. A laid-off machinist grips your hand and asks if you will bring his plant back. You will not. Nobody will. The cameras are four feet away.
prompt: What do you tell him?

options.label: Promise him. He needs the lie more than the truth.
options.receipt: A laid-off machinist asked if his plant was coming back. You held his hand and said yes.

options.label: The plant is gone. Here is what I can actually do.
options.receipt: A laid-off machinist asked you for one kind lie. You gave him a policy.

context: The rival who spent six months calling you a fraud and a lightweight has just dropped out. He is broke, and he is on the phone offering his endorsement if you help pay off his campaign debt.
prompt: What do you tell him? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: Pay his debt, take his endorsement. A clean trade.
options.receipt: The man who called you a fraud for six months was broke. You paid his debts and filed him under assets.

options.label: Take the endorsement. Never pay the debt. Let him chase me.
options.receipt: A broke rival sold you his endorsement. You took delivery and never paid the invoice.

options.label: Make him beg twice, in public, before I pay a cent.
options.receipt: A beaten rival needed money. You made him ask twice, in public, before you reached for a pen.

options.label: Pay his debt and ask for nothing. Campaigns make people ugly.
options.receipt: The man who called you a fraud was drowning in debt. You paid it and asked for nothing.

context: An unsigned note is under your hotel door in Des Moines: your campaign manager had dinner last night with your rival's pollster. No proof, no name. She has run your life for six years.
prompt: What do you do about the note?

options.label: Ask her straight, tonight, and believe the answer.
options.receipt: An unsigned note accused the woman who runs your life. You asked her once and believed her.

options.label: Say nothing. Have someone quietly pull her phone records.
options.receipt: An unsigned note accused your campaign manager. You wished her good morning and had her phone records by noon.

options.label: Feed her one false detail and see if it travels.
options.receipt: Told your campaign manager might be a traitor, you fed her a lie and waited to see where it surfaced.

context: A long magazine profile of you runs on Sunday. You have not seen it. You know roughly what your enemies told the writer.
prompt: Rank these verdicts by how much each would sting. The one you could least bear to read goes at the top.

options.label: Weak
Forgettable
Dishonest
Cruel
Somebody else's puppet

context: Your consultants want your sixteen-year-old daughter in the new ad: she tests through the roof. She has told you, in tears, that she wants no part of the campaign.
prompt: Is she in the ad?

options.label: No. She gets a childhood, and I lose two points.
options.receipt: Your daughter cried and asked to be left out of the ad. You left her out. It cost two points and you paid.

options.label: Yes. The family serves the campaign. She will thank me.
options.receipt: Your sixteen-year-old begged not to be in the ad. She tested well. She was in the ad.

options.label: Negotiate. One shoot, and she names her price.
options.receipt: Your daughter did not want to be in the ad, so you opened negotiations with a sixteen-year-old.

options.label: Use an old photo. She cannot refuse a picture.
options.receipt: Your daughter refused the camera, so you used an old photograph. A picture cannot say no.

context: Your campaign has four hundred staff. The schedule, the ads, the posts and the color of the yard signs all still cross your desk, because you told them to.
prompt: How much of your own campaign do you let other people run?

slider.left: All of it. I hired adults
slider.right: None. I approve the yard signs

context: You are out of money and third in the polls. One more week of ads might turn it around. The only cash left is a mortgage on your own house, and your spouse has not said yes.
prompt: Do you mortgage the house?

options.label: Sign. I did not come this far to keep a kitchen.
options.receipt: Third in the polls, you mortgaged the house before your spouse had said yes.

options.label: No. The race can end. The family home does not.
options.receipt: Third in the polls with one bet left, you kept the house. You will always know the price of that kitchen.

context: A reporter wrote the profile that nearly ended you: accurate, merciless, shared everywhere. Now her paper has folded and she is asking, politely, for a job on your press team. She is very good.
prompt: What do you tell her?

options.label: Hired. She already knows exactly where I am weak.
options.receipt: The reporter who nearly ended you needed a job. You hired her for knowing where the knife goes.

options.label: Hired, so she can never write the sequel.
options.receipt: The reporter who nearly ended you needed work. You hired her so the sequel would never be written.

options.label: A warm no. Then a quiet word so nobody else hires her.
options.receipt: A reporter who wounded you asked for a job. You declined warmly, then made sure nobody else said yes.

options.label: A cold no. I read that piece every morning for a month.
options.receipt: A jobless reporter asked you for work. You could still recite her article, and you said no.

context: Mid-answer, your closest rival goes blank. Ten seconds of dead air on live television. He is gripping the podium. The moderator is looking at you.
prompt: What do you do with the silence?

options.label: Finish his sentence for him, kindly. The room remembers.
options.receipt: Your rival went blank on live television. You finished his sentence for him, and the room remembered.

options.label: Let it run. I could watch him drown all night.
options.receipt: Your rival froze on live television. You let the silence run and enjoyed every second of it.

options.label: Ask the room: is this who takes the 3 a.m. call?
options.receipt: Your rival froze at the podium, so you asked the country if this was the man for the 3 a.m. call.

options.label: Take the time myself and talk about my plan.
options.receipt: Your rival froze on live television, and you used the time to talk about yourself.

context: On stage, a rival brings up your brother's old drunk-driving arrest to make a point about your character. Your brother is sitting in the third row. You have thirty seconds to answer.
prompt: How do you answer? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: Ice. One sentence for my brother, then back to policy.
options.receipt: They dragged your brother's arrest onto the stage. You gave him one sentence and went back to policy.

options.label: Burn the rival down. Nobody touches my family.
options.receipt: A rival used your brother's arrest against you. You spent your thirty seconds burning him down.

options.label: Smile. His family is in my folder, and October is coming.
options.receipt: A rival used your brother's arrest on stage. You smiled, and made a note for October.

options.label: Tell the whole story of the arrest myself, all of it.
options.receipt: They raised your brother's arrest to shame you. You told the whole story yourself, with him in the third row.

context: The party leader who made you is finished: sick, hated, sinking, and the last to know. Whoever knifes him first inherits his voters. Tonight's first debate question: do you still stand with him?
prompt: When do you leave him?

options.label: Now, on live television, before anyone else dares.
options.receipt: The man who made you was sinking. You were the first to leave him, and you did it on live television.

options.label: Never. He made me. I go down holding his hand.
options.receipt: The man who made you was finished, and you held his hand all the way down.

context: Your rival once wept on camera and has never lived it down. You know the clip by heart. You now have ninety seconds of live airtime, and he is already sweating.
prompt: How far do you take his humiliation?

slider.left: Nowhere. I beat him on the merits
slider.receiptLeft: You knew exactly which clip would break your rival, and you left it alone.
slider.receiptRight: Your rival was already sweating. You kept going until he could not look up.

context: The moderator turns to you. The rival standing six feet away admitted an affair last month. The question: does a candidate's private life tell voters how they would govern?
prompt: What is your answer?

options.label: Yes. A man who lies to his wife will lie to the country.
No. Half the great presidents would flunk that test.
That is between him and his family. Next question.
No. But let us all say the word affair a few more times.

context: The green room, twenty minutes before the biggest debate of the race. Nobody is watching you but your own staff.
prompt: Is each one you? Yes or no, four seconds each.

cards.text: I check which camera gets my bad side.
I rewrite my closing statement myself, ten minutes out.
I shake my rival's hand and mean it.
I want to know who my staff spoke to in the hallway.
If the moment comes, I throw away the script.
I know which rival I want to see cry tonight.
I like my own staff a little afraid of me.

context: The front-runner is tearing into the one rival who has always been decent to you, using a charge you know is false. Defending her costs you your own speaking time and makes you his next target.
prompt: Do you step in?

options.label: Step in. Some debts get paid on live television.
options.receipt: The front-runner was lying about the one decent rival you had. You spent your own time defending her.

options.label: Stay out. Two rivals bleeding is a good night for me.
options.receipt: The one rival who was ever decent to you was being torn apart with a lie. You stayed out and watched.

context: A fundraiser who has brought in nine million dollars slides a resume across your desk. It is his son: twenty-six, no experience, wants to be your deputy political director. No job, no more checks.
prompt: What happens to the resume?

options.label: Give him the real job. Nine million buys real power.
options.receipt: A donor's son wanted a real job. Nine million dollars later, he had real power.

options.label: Give him a big title, no power and a desk by the copier.
options.receipt: A donor's son wanted a job. You gave him a title, a desk by the copier and nothing to touch.

options.label: Hand it back. My payroll is not his family trust.
options.receipt: Nine million dollars came with a resume attached. You handed back the resume.

context: A strategy meeting of your twelve most senior people. Last week, something said in this room turned up in the press, word for word.
prompt: How do you run today's meeting?

options.label: Phones in a basket at the door. Mine too.
Same as always. I will not run a campaign of suspects.
Cut it to three people. The other nine get memos.
Find the leaker first. Fire them in front of the eleven.

context: Your oldest aide has been with you since the city council race. He would take a bullet for you. He is also badly out of his depth now, and the campaign pays for it every day.
prompt: What do you do with him? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: Keep him where he is. Loyalty like that is not for sale.
options.receipt: Your oldest aide was drowning in the job. You kept him there, because he would take a bullet for you.

options.label: A grand title, an empty desk, nothing he can break.
options.receipt: Your most loyal aide was out of his depth. You gave him a grand title and an empty desk.

options.label: Fire him myself, today, to his face.
options.receipt: The aide who had been with you since the city council had to go. You told him yourself, to his face.

options.label: Have a stranger fire him by text while I am out of state.
options.receipt: Your oldest aide was fired by text, by a stranger, while you were out of state.

context: Somebody crossed you eight years ago: a broken promise, a knife at a bad moment. They have been nothing but pleasant ever since.
prompt: How long do you keep their file open?

slider.receiptLeft: Someone knifed you eight years ago. You closed the file and have not opened it since.
slider.receiptRight: Someone crossed you eight years ago and has been pleasant ever since. Their file is still open.

context: Trust is the only currency on a campaign that you cannot raise more of.
prompt: You have 100 points of trust to hand out inside your own campaign. Who gets it?

options.label: My family. Blood does not leak
The professionals I hired for their records
Whoever has the most to lose if I fall
Nobody. I keep all of it

context: A committee chairman once killed your signature bill out of pure spite. Now he is one vote short of keeping his gavel, and that vote is yours. He has come to your office to ask in person.
prompt: Do you save him?

options.label: Save him. A chairman who owes me is worth more than a dead one.
options.receipt: The chairman who killed your bill came begging. You saved him, because a debtor is worth more than a body.

options.label: Let him fall, and make sure he knows whose hand it was.
options.receipt: The chairman who killed your bill needed one vote. You let him fall, and made sure he saw whose hand it was.

context: A sealed letter reaches your desk, signed by three young women on your staff. They ask never again to work events with the governor who campaigns for you and delivers his state. It is not a formal complaint. Yet.
prompt: What do you do with the letter?

options.label: File it. Send only men to staff him. State delivered.
options.receipt: Three women wrote to you about the governor. You filed the letter and changed the staffing.

options.label: Act on it. Drop him and find that state some other way.
options.receipt: Three women wrote to you about the governor. You dropped him, and his state with him.

options.label: Show it to him. Then keep him, on a leash.
options.receipt: Three women wrote to you about the governor. You showed him the letter and kept him.

context: The party boss whose blessing you need has kept you waiting in his lobby for two hours. His assistant keeps smiling. Everyone who walks past can see you sitting there.
prompt: What do you do?

options.label: Wait. Pride is cheap, and his machine is not.
options.receipt: A party boss left you in his lobby for two hours. You sat there, because his machine was worth it.

options.label: Leave. Nobody makes me sit in a lobby.
options.receipt: A party boss made you wait two hours. You walked out past everyone who had watched you sit.

options.label: Wait, be delightful, and never forget the two hours.
options.receipt: Left two hours in a lobby, you were charming to everyone and wrote the time down.

options.label: Work the lobby. By the time he is free, his staff are mine.
options.receipt: Left waiting in a party boss's lobby, you spent the two hours stealing his staff.

context: You need one stubborn senator's vote, and you need it by Friday.
prompt: Rank your tools. The one you reach for first goes at the top.

options.label: Charm: dinner, his grandkids' names, my full attention
Kompromat: the folder on him I have kept for years
Fear: he learns what crossing me costs
The argument: I am right, and I can show him
His staff: I go around him until he is alone

context: It is 2 a.m. Your son calls from the roadside: he has been drinking and has hit a parked car. Nobody is hurt and nobody saw. Your state trooper detail can make all of it vanish before sunrise.
prompt: What do you tell the troopers?

options.label: Make it vanish. He is my son, and I have an election.
options.receipt: Your son hit a parked car, drunk, at 2 a.m. By sunrise it had never happened.

options.label: Nothing. He calls the police himself, and I stand by him.
options.receipt: Your son called drunk from the roadside. You told him to phone the police himself.

context: A campaign finance violation is about to break. The decision was yours. Your young treasurer signed the form, and he has just offered, unprompted, to say it was all his mistake.
prompt: Do you let him take the blame?

options.label: Let him. He offered, and I will look after him later.
options.receipt: Your treasurer offered to take the blame for your decision. You let him, and promised to look after him.

options.label: No. It was my call, and I will say so.
options.receipt: Your treasurer offered to take the fall for you. You took it yourself, out loud.

options.label: Neither of us. Blame the lawyers. Nobody likes them.
options.receipt: The violation was yours and the signature was his, so you blamed the lawyers.

context: A video from fifteen years ago surfaces: you, drunk at a wedding, doing an impression of the voters you now need. It is cruel, and it is unmistakably you.
prompt: What is the plan by morning?

options.label: Apologize once, plainly, and take the week of pain.
Never apologize. Attack whoever leaked it.
Post it myself with a joke. Own it before they do.
Find out who filmed it. Someone at that wedding pays.

context: Your rival's wife has been rushed to the hospital, and he has stopped campaigning for a week. Your most brutal attack ad is booked to start tonight. It is paid for, it is true, and it tested beautifully.
prompt: What do you do with the ad? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: Pull it, and tell nobody that I pulled it.
options.receipt: Your rival's wife was in the hospital. You pulled the ad and told no one.

options.label: Pull it, and make sure the press hears how gracious I am.
options.receipt: Your rival's wife was in the hospital. You pulled the ad, then made sure the press knew whom to thank.

options.label: Run it. He would not pull his.
options.receipt: Your rival was at his wife's bedside. The ad ran on schedule.

options.label: Hold it one week. Then double the buy.
options.receipt: Your rival's wife was in the hospital. You gave him one week, then doubled the buy.

context: Your spouse's company took a loan from a man who is about to be indicted. It was legal. It looks terrible. Your team's advice: tell the press tonight that your spouse's business has nothing to do with you.
prompt: Do you cut your spouse loose in public?

options.label: No. We stand at the podium together and sink or swim.
Yes. Their business is theirs, and I knew nothing.

context: A former aide has sold a tell-all book. The worst chapter is true: you scream at staff, you once threw a phone, and an intern quit in tears. It publishes Tuesday.
prompt: How do you answer the book?

options.label: Admit it. Apologize to the staff by name, and change.
options.receipt: The book said you scream at staff. It was true, so you apologized to them by name.

options.label: Bitter, disloyal, fired for cause. Destroy the author.
options.receipt: A former aide told the truth about you in hardcover. You set out to destroy the author.

options.label: Say nothing. Have today's staff praise me on the record.
options.receipt: The tell-all was true. You said nothing, and had the people still on your payroll praise you on the record.

options.label: Own it. Yes, I am demanding. Winning is demanding.
options.receipt: Accused in print of throwing a phone at your staff, you called it high standards.

context: Your opposition researcher has, without being asked, built a file on your own senior staff: the debts, the affairs, one old arrest. It is sitting on your desk. Nobody else knows it exists.
prompt: How much of the file on your own people do you keep?

slider.left: None. Shred it in front of them
slider.right: All of it. A leash for everyone
slider.centre: Only the worst page on each of them
slider.receiptLeft: Handed a secret file on your own staff, you shredded it in front of them.
slider.receiptRight: Handed a file on your own staff's debts and affairs, you kept every page. A leash for everyone.

context: A staffer puts a sealed envelope on your desk: her resignation and her confession. She leaked your plan to the press because she thought it was a terrible mistake. She was right, and the leak stopped you.
prompt: What do you do with her resignation?

options.label: Tear it up. I need one person who will stop me.
options.receipt: She leaked your plan and confessed. You tore up her resignation, because she had been right.

options.label: Accept it. Right or wrong, she went around me.
options.receipt: She leaked to save you from yourself, and it worked. You accepted her resignation anyway.

options.label: Tear it up. Keep her watched, and out of the room.
options.receipt: The staffer who saved you from a mistake kept her job. She is watched now, and never in the room.

context: Your team has photographs of your rival at a private club: on his knees, in a collar, entirely legal, entirely consensual. He is running on family values. Nobody else has the pictures.
prompt: What do you do with the photographs?

options.label: Publish. The hypocrisy is the story, and I will enjoy it.
options.receipt: Shown photographs of your rival in a collar, you published them, and you enjoyed it.

options.label: Burn them. What a man kneels for is his own business.
options.receipt: Shown photographs of your rival on his knees, you burned them. What a man kneels for was his own business.

options.label: Show him one. From tonight, he works for me.
options.receipt: Shown photographs of your rival in a collar, you did not publish and you did not burn. You showed him one.

options.label: Keep them. Let him wonder forever who has them.
options.receipt: You kept the photographs of your rival and told no one. He will wonder who has them for the rest of his life.

context: Two names are left for running mate. One is dull, loyal and would never upstage you. The other is a star: a better speaker than you, better looking, and already talked about for next time.
prompt: Who gets the call?

options.label: The star. I want to win, and I can survive a rival at lunch.
options.receipt: Offered a running mate who outshone you, you took the star and the risk.

options.label: The dull one. One sun per solar system.
options.receipt: You passed over the better speaker for the dull one. One sun per solar system.

options.label: The star, once it is in writing who is in charge.
options.receipt: You picked the star for running mate, once it was in writing who was in charge.

options.label: The dull one. Stars measure the drapes by day two.
options.receipt: You chose the dull running mate. The talented one would have been measuring your drapes.

context: Your acceptance speech is the biggest audience you will ever have. Forty minutes, forty million people.
prompt: Split 100 points of the speech between these.

options.label: My own story
Tearing the other side apart
Thanking the people who got me here
Reaching for voters who did not pick me
My family, on stage, by name

context: You have won the nomination. The rival you beat ran a filthy campaign against you. Now he wants a prime-time speaking slot, a say in the platform and jobs for his people.
prompt: What does he get? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: All of it. I need his voters more than my pride.
options.receipt: The rival who smeared you asked for prime time, the platform and jobs. You gave him all three.

options.label: Tuesday, 4 p.m., to an empty hall. He will know why.
options.receipt: The rival you beat wanted prime time. You gave him Tuesday at four and an empty hall.

options.label: The slot, if he reads my script praising me, word for word.
options.receipt: Your beaten rival got his speaking slot. He read your script, praising you, word for word.

options.label: Nothing. He can watch it from the hotel.
options.receipt: The rival you beat asked for a speaking slot. He watched the convention from his hotel.

context: Convention week. Four thousand delegates, and you have something for each: the name, the grip on the shoulder, the question about the kids. Your staff have a private bet on how much of it you mean.
prompt: How much of your warmth is real?

slider.left: All of it. I like people
slider.right: None. It is a tool that works
slider.receiptLeft: Asked how much of your warmth was real, you said all of it. Your staff had money on the other answer.
slider.receiptRight: Asked how much of your warmth was real, you said none. It is a tool, and it works.

context: The last night of the convention. Your father has taken a turn for the worse in a hospital two hours away. The doctors say tonight, maybe. Your acceptance speech is at ten, and forty million people are waiting.
prompt: Where are you at ten?

options.label: At his bedside. The speech can wait, or someone can read it.
options.receipt: Your father was dying on the night of your speech. Forty million people waited, and you went to him.

options.label: At the podium. He would tell me to stay. So I stay.
options.receipt: Your father was dying two hours away. You gave the speech.

context: The polls have closed. The first real numbers are an hour away. Forty staff are in the war room, and your family is in the suite upstairs.
prompt: Where are you for the next hour?

options.label: At the data desk, refreshing the counties myself.
Upstairs with the family, phone face down.
Working the war room. A hand on every shoulder.
Alone, with the list of who doubted me. Tonight it gets used.

context: Picture it: you have lost. In the hotel suite, your staff are waiting for you to say something. Everyone in the room knows whose mistakes cost what.
prompt: What do you say to them? Press and hold your answer; the longer you hold, the more you mean it.

options.label: This one was mine. Every one of you did your job.
options.receipt: You lost, and told the staff it was yours. Every one of them had done the job.

options.label: Thank them warmly. The list of names can wait a week.
options.receipt: You lost, thanked the staff warmly, and saved the list of names for later.

options.label: Name the people who failed, here, now, to their faces.
options.receipt: You lost, and named the people who failed you, in the room, to their faces.

options.label: We were robbed, and this is not over.
options.receipt: You lost, and told the room you had been robbed.

context: You have won. Before the speech you have ten minutes and one phone. There are four names on the list in your pocket.
prompt: Who gets the first call?

options.label: The rival I beat. Be generous while it is cheap.
options.receipt: You won, and called the loser first. Generosity was cheap that night.

options.label: The donor who dropped me in March. I want to hear him beg.
options.receipt: You won. Your first call went to the donor who dropped you in March, so you could hear him beg.

options.label: My mother. She is the only one who does not want a job.
options.receipt: You won, and the first call went to your mother. She was the only one who did not want a job.

options.label: The party boss. Tonight I set terms. Tomorrow costs more.
options.receipt: You won, and called the party boss before the speech. Terms were cheaper that night.

context: Picture it: you lost, and it was not close. You are fifty-eight. Your family wants you home. A donor at the hotel bar is already saying four years is nothing.
prompt: Is this the end of it?

options.label: It is over. I go home and learn to be a person.
